Copy
KOP-y
n.
From Latin copia, plenty, abundance — a transcript being a multiplying of the original. Webster 1828: a transcript from an original; an imitation or resemblance. Deuteronomy requires a king to make one with his own hand, and the requirement is a doctrine of government.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

The law of the king in Deuteronomy is remarkable for what it commands a monarch to do personally: when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites (Deuteronomy 17:18). Not commission a copy — write one. The following verses say it shall be with him and he shall read therein all the days of his life, that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren. The sovereign is placed under a text he has transcribed by hand. Joshua carries out the public counterpart on Ebal: he wrote there upon the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he wrote in the presence of the children of Israel (Joshua 8:32). Copying is likewise how the wisdom literature reached us: These are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out (Proverbs 25:1) — a note preserved in the canon about the canon’s own transmission. And Ezra’s opponents send their accusation in the same form: This is the copy of the letter that they sent unto him, even unto Artaxerxes the king (Ezra 4:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines COPY as a transcript from an original writing; an imitation, likeness or reproduction; a pattern or example to be imitated.

expand to see more

COPY, n. — A transcript from an original writing; hence, a writing like another.

An imitation, likeness or reproduction of an original.

A pattern; an example proposed for imitation; as, a copy set for a learner.

COPY, v.t. — To write, print or engrave according to an original; to transcribe; to imitate.

Latin copia, plenty — a transcript multiplying the original.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 17:18 — "And it shall be, when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites:"

Joshua 8:32 — "And he wrote there upon the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he wrote in the presence of the children of Israel."

Proverbs 25:1 — "These are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out."

Deuteronomy 17:19 — "And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:"

Modern Corruption

Deuteronomy 17:18-19 places the highest civil authority under a written law he must copy and read for life, which is the biblical root of limited government and the standing answer to every claim of absolute sovereignty.

expand to see more

The king of Israel is not the source of law; he is a reader of it, and he is required to produce the text in his own handwriting so that no distance can open between the ruler and the rule. The purpose clause is explicit — that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren — which makes this the earliest statement of a principle later Reformed political thought would develop at length: authority is delegated, bounded, and answerable to a higher law it did not make. Samuel Rutherford’s Lex Rex argues the case from precisely such texts, against the divine right of kings as an absolute claim, and the Reformed doctrine of the lesser magistrate follows from it. This dictionary affirms the lordship of Christ over every sphere and the classical two-kingdoms distinction while rejecting the Radical Two-Kingdoms position that would remove God’s law from the magistrate’s horizon altogether.

Proverbs 25:1 is a small verse with a large use: the canon itself records that Hezekiah’s men copied out an earlier collection. Scripture is not embarrassed by its own transmission, and the modern habit of treating the existence of copyists and collections as evidence against inspiration mistakes the doctrine. Verbal plenary inspiration attaches to the original autographs; providential preservation is what has carried the text to us through exactly such labour as Hezekiah’s men performed. The 1689 Confession states both together — the Scriptures were immediately inspired by God, and by His singular care and providence kept pure in all ages. A copy faithfully made is not a diluted original; it is how the original reaches the reader.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mishneh (H4932), a double or copy; parshegen (H6572), a copy or transcript; Greek antigraphon, a copy; the Septuagint’s rendering of mishneh here gave the book of Deuteronomy its name.

expand to see more

Hebrew mishneh (H4932) — a double, a second, a copy; a copy of this law (Deuteronomy 17:18) and on the stones at Ebal (Joshua 8:32).

Greek deuteronomion — the second law, the Septuagint’s rendering of mishneh hattorah, which supplied the English name of the book.

Hebrew parshegen (H6572) — a copy or transcript of a document; the copy of the letter (Ezra 4:11).

Hebrew athaq (H6275) — to move or transcribe; which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out (Proverbs 25:1).

Hebrew torah (H8451) — the law, the thing copied and read all the days of the king’s life.

Usage

"He shall write him a copy of this law in a book (Deuteronomy 17:18) — not commission a copy; write one."

"That he may learn to fear the LORD his God (Deuteronomy 17:19) — the sovereign placed under a text by his own hand."

"Which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out (Proverbs 25:1) — the canon recording its own transmission."
